claims.text: A controlled two-step thermomechanical process can form independently controllable coherent δ-lamellae and γ″ precipitates in a dual-phase BCC/FCC high-entropy alloy.
The two-step process can simultaneously improve strength and ductility relative to an as-cast or homogenized microstructure.
The two-step process can simultaneously improve Young’s modulus and fracture resistance relative to an as-cast or homogenized microstructure.

Conventional cast or homogenized dual-phase HEAs have coarse microstructures containing continuous brittle regions or non-optimized precipitate distributions that limit ductility and fracture resistance.
Hot rolling induces formation of δ-lamellae.
Cold rolling followed by controlled annealing and aging near 650 °C nucleates a uniform distribution of fine, coherent γ″ particles.
Temperatures below the over-aging regime, together with controlled strain and cooling rates, preserve precipitate size and interfacial coherency.
The method should work in dual-phase BCC/FCC HEAs capable of forming coherent precipitates.
The method should not provide the proposed benefits in alloys prone to excessive deleterious brittle or incoherent intermetallic phases.
Coherent δ-lamellae and γ″ particles impede dislocation motion while mitigating stress concentration.
The precipitates create a refined, heterogeneous microstructure that distributes strain uniformly.
Coherent precipitate interfaces produce order hardening by impeding dislocation glide while permitting gradual dislocation transmission across phase boundaries.
Deformation-induced grain refinement increases yield strength through Hall–Petch strengthening.
Deformation-induced grain refinement enhances Young’s modulus through grain-boundary strengthening.
Well-dispersed hard phases arrest crack initiation and propagation and thereby improve fracture resistance.
The treatment will increase yield strength by more than 50% relative to untreated material.
The treatment will increase fracture strain by at least 20% relative to untreated material.
The treatment will measurably increase effective Young’s modulus and fracture toughness.
The desired benefits may disappear if processing temperatures exceed the stability range of the target precipitates.
Direct evidence quantifying Young’s-modulus and fracture-resistance improvements from the proposed interfaces is limited, and residual stresses may affect those properties.
